About your goods; yet Job did not swell against God in these, but said humbly what he had truly done; often the just and the unjust have the same words, and what pleases in the one offends in the other, as the Pharisee who justifies himself in work (Luke 18), and Hezekiah who justifies himself in thought (2 Kings 20).
15.14: 15.14 What is man? By the very fact that he is called man, earthly and weak is expressed. For he is named from the ground. And that one born of woman may appear just, etc. For how should he appear just who is born of her who was the giver of injustice? Indeed, the woman first gave injustice to the man in paradise.
15.15: 15.15 And the heavens are not clean. By this name of the heavens he repeated what he signified by the name of the saints, who before the strict judgment of God cannot themselves be perfectly clean.
15.16: 15.16 How much more abominable. Same place. Any perverse man is abominable because of the uncleanness of the stain. Unprofitable, because of the justice of a perfect life; he is said to drink iniquity, because what is drunk has no delay for swallowing. Guilt, therefore, since it is committed by the unjust man without any reconsideration, is drunk like water as iniquity.
15.17: 15.17 I will show you. Because he teaches with less authority who speaks of what he heard than he who speaks of what he had seen, that Eliphaz might arrogate to himself the stronger authority, he says: What I have seen I will tell you. It is the mark of the arrogant, etc., up to 'which he fortifies by the authority of the Fathers.'
15.18: 15.18 The wise confess. Behold the boldness of heretics, etc., up to 'a stranger, that is the devil, has passed through their hearts.' Behold the sayings.
15.20: 15.20 All his days. The elect too are wont on certain days to be proud, but before they end life they change their hearts from elation; the wicked man is proud all his days, and so ends his life as not to recede at all from elation. And the number of years of his tyranny. A tyrant properly, etc., up to 'whose life is held in uncertainty?'
15.21: 15.21 A sound of dread is always in his ears. Same place. The perverse mind is always in labors, as the good is always tranquil: because it either contrives evils to inflict, or fears lest these be inflicted on it by others.
15.22: 15.22 He believes not that he can return from darkness to: because, while he believes himself struck on every side by ambushes, salvation being despaired of, he always grows toward wickedness.
15.23: 15.23 When he stirs, etc. Bread here is the stipend of the present life, etc., up to 'conquered by avarice, he despises those things.'
15.24: 15.24 Tribulation shall terrify him, etc. In everything the wicked man does, etc., up to 'if perhaps there be lacking to him something he may oppose by deceit.'
15.25: 15.25 He stretched out, etc. Same place. To stretch out the hand against God, etc., up to 'is now done by many individually.'
15.26: 15.26 He ran, that is, in evil work he had no obstacle from adversity. And is armed with a fat neck. The fat neck is rich pride, propped by abundant goods as by much flesh.
15.27: 15.27 Fatness has covered his face. Thickness covers the face, because the abundance of desired earthly things presses the eyes of the mind. And from his sides. Same place. The sides of the rich are those who cling to them; the fat hangs from his sides, because whoever clings to a powerful and wicked man also swells with his power as from fatness.
15.28: 15.28 He has dwelt in cities. Because a city is named from the conversation of those living together, etc., up to 'they show without doubt that they have fallen from the building of life.'
15.29: 15.29 He shall not be enriched, because the thought of the proud man will not be inhabited by the grace of its author. Nor shall he continue. Same place. As if he said: What he seems to have passes outwardly, and what could not pass he has not within. Nor shall he send root into the earth, because as at a light breath, so at the movement of a hidden sentence his life is plucked up; or, 'he will not send into the earth,' etc., because he never plants the thought of his heart in the desire of eternal life.
15.30: 15.30 He shall not depart out of darkness. Because he does not seek the light of justice, he does not depart from darkness. His branches, etc. Because those too who are joined to him burn with earthly desires, so that they do not bear fruit of good work, because through wickedness they pant after the lowest things. And he shall be taken away by the spirit, because he will receive the sentence of the stroke by the same by which he does not restrain the breath of his mouth with the fear of God.
15.31: 15.31 He shall not believe. Because almsgiving redeems him, etc., up to 'because it does not redeem the soul which it does not restrain from vices.'
15.32: 15.32 Before his days. Gregory. Because long in mind, etc., up to 'death meets the undisciplined.'
15.33: 15.33 His hands are dried up from every good working. He shall be hurt as, etc. If a flourishing vineyard, etc., up to 'in holy zeal makes them strangers to fruit,' hence he adds: And like an olive tree casting off. The olive when in flower, etc., up to 'so that they cannot discern with what intention they do what.' Or in the first flower. The weak ought not to rule or do lower things, because he grows cold in earthly acts. Or, when he sees that what he does pleases, he does the same good works more ardently, and as it were glows in holy zeal, and so perishes from the heat.
15.34: 15.34 For the congregation of the hypocrite, etc. Hypocrites gather good works, but their very gathering is barren, because by what they do they do not seek to receive fruit in eternal retribution. And fire shall devour their tabernacles, etc. He calls tabernacles the bodies in which their souls dwell: which the desire of praise burns here, and afterward the fire of Gehenna will consume. Tabernacles. Thought is the tabernacle in which the mind dwells, which the heat of avarice lays waste. Or he calls the heart a tabernacle, which the ardor of praise consumes. Or the body is the tabernacle of the soul, and those who burn here in mind will burn in flesh with the fires of Gehenna.
15.35: 15.35 He conceived sorrow. When he thinks perverse things he gives birth to iniquity; when he has begun to fulfil them, he has conceived. The mind of the hypocrite too is never free from evil, because what he seeks he envies others, from whose despite he would be more illustrious, and so he prepares snares that he alone may gain esteem. His womb prepares deceits, that is, the mind, in which thoughts are generated, conceives greater malice against neighbors, the more he seeks to be seen alone above all as more innocent: he says this because he thought Job was struck for hypocrisy.
16.2: 16.2 I have often heard such things. The elect often hear the evils of others as their own, and the charge is laid on them by those by whom the charged crimes are committed. Burdensome comforters are you all. The perverse, when the good labor, etc., up to 'lest he who ought to soothe the pain increase it.'
16.3: 16.3 Shall windy words have an end? The wicked utter windy words. For their sayings, though sometimes sound in sense, are nevertheless inflated by elation. Or is it anything troublesome to you if you speak? As if he said: because you speak the more, since you hear nothing troublesome from me about your action.
16.4: 16.4 I also could speak like you. He tells what he could have done, but lest he abandon justice he declines what he could do.
16.5: 16.5 Oh that your soul were for my soul. In these words it is shown that he intends, etc., up to 'because he would rebuke their evils with moderate invective.'
16.6: 16.6 As though sparing. Note 'as though,' because, etc., up to 'he seems to approve, and they grow into an example.'
16.8: 16.8 But now sorrow has oppressed me, etc. Same place. The Church is pressed by sorrow, etc., up to 'those whom she has within'; hence in the voice of the blessed man there is fittingly added at once.
16.9: 16.9 My wrinkles, etc. The wrinkles of the Church are all who live doubly in her, who proclaim the faith with their voices and deny it by their works. In time of peace, because they see the same faith to be an honor with the powers of this world, they pretend to be faithful: but when adversity suddenly troubles the Church, they at once show what they contrive in a faithless mind. And the sense is: they rebuke me by pursuing me, who, placed in my body, do not amend the malice of their duplicity. And a false speaker rises up against my face, etc. Same place. While they do not presume to contradict her preaching openly, the Church suffers falsehood as if behind her back; but when the time of malice has broken out, he who now disparages through fear comes to contradict to her face: because he opposes the words of the true faith with open voices. And since this is done by the malignant spirit, he turns the words to describe him.
16.10: 16.10 He has gathered his fury. The devil, prince of false speech, has now fury against the Church, but it is scattered, because he stirs secret temptations through individuals. But when, permission received, he rages openly against her, he gathers his fury against her, because he binds himself with his whole intention to her affliction. He gnashes his teeth against her and looks on her with terrible eyes, because through some he exercises cruelties against her and through others provides what he may exercise.
16.11: 16.11 They have opened their mouths upon me, etc. Same place. Because the reprobate open their mouths in reproaching when they do not fear to preach error and deride the preachings of the right faith. They have struck my cheek. The cheek of the Church are the holy preachers, who convert the life of the carnal by the word of correction: these the reprobate persecute especially, and while they even kill them, that punishment satisfies them which especially torments or chastens the mind of the Church. My cheek. Peter is the cheek, who slays and eats. Samson holds the jawbone of an ass and slays enemies, that is, Christ holds the simple heralds by the hand of virtue and slays the carnal from their vices. The jawbone is cast to the ground, it pours forth waters: because the bodies of the heralds given to death show great miracles.
16.12: 16.12 God has shut me up, etc. The people of the elect is shut up with the wicked man when its flesh is given for a time to the persecutions of the ancient enemy. It is handed over not in spirit but to the hands of enemies, because the less they can seize it in mind, the more cruelly they burn against its flesh.
16.13: 16.13 I who was once wealthy. Gregory. He designates the mind of the weak, because while they do not know how to foresee adversities, these are the heavier on them, the more unexpectedly they are borne. Or, in certain ones, these same slipping backward, this Church suffers, who after wealth of doctrine are sometimes turned by sudden vices. He has held my neck. The neck here signifies the uprightness of liberty, which the enemy holds in time of persecution; he binds it while the weak do not presume to preach freely the true things they feel. Or he calls his neck those who in the Church, under pretext of defending uprightness, serve the vice of elation: which the enemy bends by the strictness of his persecution. And has set me up as a mark. Same place. A mark is set up to be struck by the discharge of arrows. The faithful people is therefore set as a mark for its enemy, because he always assails it with his blows, afflicts it with his persecutions, hence the Apostle: 'For you yourselves know that we are appointed to this' (1 Thessalonians 3). As if he said plainly: Why do you marvel at our wounds in this time? If we seek eternal joys, we have come to this to be struck.
16.14: 16.14 He has compassed me. The Church is compassed with lances by her enemy, when in her members she is assailed on every side by the crafty assailant with the darts of temptations. He has wounded my loins. When the enemy draws the faithful people to luxury, he strikes it in the loins. He is said to wound together, because what he evilly suggests to us we, following, fulfil of our own will, and as it were wound ourselves together with him. He has not spared and has poured out my bowels on the ground. By the bowels of the Church he means the minds of those who contain her mysteries in themselves: whom, while the ancient enemy draws them to worldly business, he pours out her bowels on the ground. He has not spared, that is, has not desisted.
16.15: 16.15 He has cut me down. The Church in her weak ones, etc., up to 'when guilt has heaped up guilt.' He rushed upon me like a giant. Because the malignant spirit fights against this, that is the soul, overcome by evil habit, after the manner of a giant, because the more often the soul submits to him, the more intolerable it makes him to itself. But because for the most part it returns to repentance, there follows.
16.16: 16.16 I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin. In sackcloth and ashes penance is understood, in skin and flesh the sin of the flesh. Therefore sackcloth is sewed upon the skin, and the flesh is covered with ashes, because the guilt of the flesh is covered by penance, lest in the examination of the strict judge it be seen for vengeance. My face is swollen. The face of the Church are those who, placed in government, appear first, that the honor of the faithful people may come from their appearance. They lament the faults of the weak; but when they see some return to pardon, and some persist in iniquity, they are stunned at the hidden judgments of God, which they do not understand.
16.17: 16.17 And my eyelids. They are called eyelids because they watch to provide for the journeys of the people; but when even watchful leaders do not understand the hidden judgments of God, the eyelids of the holy Church grow dim.
16.18: 16.18 I have suffered these things. From the words of the body, etc., up to 'by whom is the sorrow borne?'
16.19: 16.19 O earth, cover not my blood. To sinning man it was said: 'You are earth, and to earth you shall go'; this earth does not hide the blood of our Redeemer, because every sinner, taking the price of his redemption, confesses and praises it, and makes it known to the neighbors he can. The earth also did not cover his blood: because holy Church has already preached the mystery of her redemption in all parts of the world. And let my cry find in you no place to hide. Same place. The cry of our Redeemer is the blood of redemption, which is received by the faithful, which, as the Apostle says, speaks better than the blood of Abel: because the blood of Abel asked the death of the fratricide, the blood of the Lord obtained life for persecutors. This cry finds a place to hide in us, if what the mind has believed the tongue keeps silent.
1.13: 1.13 Now on a certain day, when his sons and daughters, etc. The apostles and all the faithful. The elder son is the Jewish people, begotten by the law; the younger, the Gentile people, called at the end. In the house of the firstborn, then, the apostles feast, because as yet they were feeding on the delights of Sacred Scripture in the gathering of the Jewish people alone, to whom it was then said: 'Go not into the way of the Gentiles' (Matthew 10). They were eating and drinking, etc. To eat is to rejoice in good works; to drink wine is to glow with heavenly desire. Of their firstborn brother, etc. Wisdom is born first in the heart, etc., up to 'that the afflicted mind may recover what, preoccupied, it lost.'
1.14: 1.14 The oxen were plowing, etc. Same place. The plowing oxen are the good working well; the she-asses, those living simply; these feed beside the oxen, because they are nourished by their understanding. The Sabeans taking captive, that is, demons, the servants, that is, beginners not yet of manly constancy, with the sword, that is, with despair of eternity. The messenger who escapes is the prophetic word, which says: 'My people is led away captive, because they had no knowledge' (Isaiah 5); because when the evils he foretold come to pass, he returns to the Lord as one made sound; for when the weak are taken captive, he is recognized as having foretold true things.
1.15: 1.15 And the servants. He calls 'servants' that caution of diligence by which he provides for these things, and which is also struck in him.
1.16: 1.16 The fire of God fell from heaven. 'Heaven' means the teachers of the law, the priests, from whom the fire of envy falls upon the sheep and the servants, that is, the innocent and the weak. The servant returns sound, because the prophecy was shown to have spoken truly; zeal seizes the uninstructed people. Same place. The sheep are the innocence of thoughts. Fire from heaven, that is, from the aerial powers the flame of spite rushes in, and often kindles clean thoughts with the heat of lust; and this fire is God's, not by his doing but by his permitting; and because watchfulness is overwhelmed by a sudden impulse, the guardian servants are killed. But discernment alone, that is, reason, reports the losses to the mind, and as it were calls the Lord to lamentation.
1.17: 1.17 The Chaldeans made, etc. 'Chaldeans' is interpreted 'fierce,' etc., up to 'these struck the servants with the sword,' that is, by a sinister persuasion, etc. The camels, etc. The camel is an animal partly clean, etc., up to 'and discernment alone reports to the mind what to weep over.' That I might tell you, etc. Evils are reported, and many, and sudden, so that, a wound being laid upon a wound, he may bear it impatiently; and the cunning enemy tries him not so much by the loss of goods as by the order of the messages. First he reports the lesser misfortunes, then greater ones, finally the death of his sons, lest the loss of goods should seem cheap to one already bereaved, since there were no heirs for whom he might keep them. Step by step, therefore, he hears worse things, so that every wound may find a place in his heart.
1.18: 1.18 Your sons, etc. Gregory. The sons and daughters, as has been said, are the apostles and the subject people, who fed on Scripture in Judea. The wind, that is, a strong temptation, bursts forth from the desert, that is, from the hearts of the Jews or from unclean spirits; and it shook the four corners on which the house stands: the priests, the scribes, the elders of the people, the Pharisees. The house, that is, Judea, falling in the persecution of the Lord, overwhelmed the apostles in despair. And the saying about the persecuting people is true: 'My beloved has done many wicked deeds in my house' (Jeremiah 11); and about the apostles: 'My neighbors stood afar off' (Psalm 37). And: 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered' (Matthew 26), etc. In the house of the brother, that is, at the feast of the elder brother, Satan overwhelmed the sons, because through the negligence of the elders he seeks entrance to the death of the younger; and he gains strength against others the more when he sees that those who by their guardianship are set over others are serving gaiety. They were not indeed given over to the belly; but when the good intention of the mind burns less amid feasts, it foresees less.
1.19: 1.19 Suddenly a wind. Same place. He is said to have secretly moved the elements against him, he by whose nod they are moved: although the devil, having once received power from God, may shake the elements for the use of his wickedness, as fire and water serve the use of those condemned to the mine. From the region of the desert. The region of the desert, etc., up to 'the wind rushes in, showing the named wrath in the air.'
1.20: 1.20 Then Job arose, and rent his garments. Same place. When the house fell, etc., up to 'that the whole heart, burning in the love of God, may consume them by the perfection of devotion.' And having shaved his head. It is thought great constancy, etc., up to 'and he showed that he consented to the divine power.' Falling to the ground. Gregory. Falling, he worshiped, because he offers true prayer who humbly sees that he is dust. Hence he also says: Naked I came out of my mother's womb. First grace begot him naked in faith, and the same receives him naked. When, struck by vices, he flees naked, as it were, to mercy, and having at some time been laid bare of some virtue, he is better clothed by humility itself, attributing to God and not to himself what he has: the Lord gave the goods, the Lord also takes them away, which is done for a time so that the humble man may possess them better.
1.21: 1.21 Naked I came out. Naked the earth brought me forth as I entered here, naked the earth will receive me as I depart. A consolation from the condition of things: that he has not lost what was his own, but recalls that it was received and to be left behind; he foresees the time when he did not yet have these things, and what sort he will be when he departs. He also consoles himself from the justice of God. From my mother's womb. The mother of Christ is the Synagogue, which held him covered in itself by the letter, and did not see him naked in his divinity, but from her he came naked to the Gentiles. Behold Joseph, whom the Synagogue, believing him a mere man, wished to bind in an adulterous embrace: he left to her the covering of the letter and showed himself plainly to the Gentiles. But he will return naked, when at the end of the world God will become known to the remnant of Israel. The Lord gave. Judea, while she believed he was to come, took away, when she herself despised him as he came. As it pleased the Lord. When we are troubled, we ought to run back to the judgment of God and to render greater praises, because we know ourselves more truly to be struck.
1.22: 1.22 In all these things Job did not sin. Same place. A grieving mind ought to guard itself, etc., up to 'his heart did not swell, his mouth did not murmur, his tongue was not rebellious.'
2.1: 2.1 And it came to pass, etc. Whence do you come? Gregory, on Job, book 3. This not as before, etc., up to 'you who wished to diminish, served his advancement.'
2.3: 2.3 Innocence. He retains innocence who, even after a fall, roused by a spark of reason, repents faithfully. Same place. How was the Father moved against Christ, with whom he is the same, through Satan? Because Christ as man would not have suffered had Adam not sinned; when Satan moved Adam, he moved against Christ God. In vain, because he bore the penalty without guilt of his own; but not in vain, because he paid what another had seized.
2.4: 2.4 Skin for skin. The devil thought the Son of God, on account of the miracles, to be God's Son, but on account of his lowly things a mere man. Judging him therefore from others, who in the place of shepherds despise the losses of others, as though unmoved by many things taken away, he tempts him by the pain of his own flesh, as though one who does not grieve for others might grieve for himself. When he asks this to be done, he speaks through desires; these he inflicted through the members with words and desires, through which he said: 'Let us put wood into his bread' (Jeremiah 11), that is, by fixing his body let us apply the stake of the cross. Same place. Skin is given for skin, because often, when a blow comes at the eye, we put up the hand so that we may be wounded in it rather than in the more tender part: knowing this is customarily done, he says: Skin for skin, and all that a man has. As if to say, Job endures so many scourges outside himself with equanimity because he fears being struck himself; and from care for himself he feels less about his own possessions; hence he seeks to strike him: Put forth your hand, which God rightly permits, so that the often-defeated one may fall silent.
2.5: 2.5 But put forth your hand. Often the devil, after assaulting the mind, ceases for a time in order to break suddenly upon it when it is secure; therefore he asks again for Job, which God grants by being silent. And touch his mouth. By the mouth and flesh he means bodily life, by the soul he means reason, as above.
2.6: 2.6 Behold, he is in your hand. Satan had power through his own over the flesh of Christ, but he spares the soul, not because he does not tempt it, but because he does not overcome it; or he loses the soul, that is, the dear and chosen ones, from his own right, when he kills him from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head: because from the beginning of the world he inflicted hard things on his members, and by raging came even to their head, that is, Christ. Behold, he is in your hand. He allows us to be tempted, that we may seem weak to ourselves, and yet he guards us.
2.7: 2.7 So Satan went out. Gregory. Having received permission, etc., up to 'looks back by repenting, lest any elation arise.'
2.8: 2.8 Who scraped the corruption with a potsherd. Same place. A potsherd is made of clay, etc., up to 'but worse are those who are in elation, like Job's wife, who proudly persuades her husband.'
2.9: 2.9 And his wife said to him. Same place. He shows the devil's first temptation, etc., up to 'but they slide into harshness.' Do you still continue in your simplicity? She charges him with simplicity, because he despises earthly things and desires eternal ones, as if she said: Why do you simply seek eternal things and groan wrongly over these? Giving up the eternal, despise present evils, or escape by dying. But those men suffered these things as a pattern of uprightness. Hence he says: As one of the foolish women, etc.; they endure those who strike them from outside, they teach the perverse within: there they are strong, here merciful; there they repel adversaries, here they protect their own; and it is a great thing in battle to do both. Do you still continue? Eve repeats her words, as though saying: Abandon simplicity, that is, obedience; despise the forbidden by eating it. Bless God and die. That is, by transgressing the command, live beyond what you were created. See the order: after the wounds the enemy brought words, because when the force of pain grows heavy, a small persuasion more easily takes hold of someone; for this reason he who took away everything else kept the wife.
2.10: 2.10 As one of the foolish women, etc. Gregory. Because the fault lies in the mind, not in the sex: he does not say 'one of the women,' but 'of the foolish women': that she thinks perversely belongs to an accidental folly, not to the condition of nature. If we have received good things, etc. Same place. It is a great consolation in evils to remember good things, so that there may not be complete despair, just as in prosperity foresight of evil tempers elation. Hence it is said: 'In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils, and in the day of evils be not unmindful of good things.' If good things, that is, if we tend toward eternal goods, why do we not bear present evils? In all these things, etc. Same place. We sin with our lips in two ways, when we do not say just things, or when we are silent about just things. But Job neither spoke proud words against the one striking him, nor was silent about what was right against the one persuading him. He had patience, giving thanks to God, and taught his wife's folly by rebuking it; and so the enemy, thus defeated, is stirred up more ardently, and because the wife was silent, he roused others to insults. In all. Thus the saints, in all that they suffer outwardly and inwardly, neither go beyond bounds in wrongs against God, nor in insults against the perverse.
2.11: 2.11 Therefore. Same place. The friends signify the heretics, etc., up to 'hypocrites, unwilling to be but wishing to seem learned.' Hearing. It does not say 'hearing' because they hear of these vices, but the devil, who tempts through them, understands them. Three friends. This number, moral or mystical, signifies the three bands of the Chaldeans, that is, the assault that is made in deed, tongue and thought, for he assails all these. They had agreed, etc. Same place. Because they agree in falsehood, and while they teach their own things, they seem to console. But those truly console in present affliction who instruct about eternal things. Heretics are called friends, because they are to be named so not from their own wickedness but from our kindness: as 'Friend, why have you come?' (Matthew 26). They had agreed. Because certain vices are joined together against us among themselves, such as pride and anger, laxity and fear: which, though different, tend to the same end, that is, the subversion of the spiritual Job.
2.12: 2.12 And when they had lifted up their eyes afar off. Those who are low lift up their eyes, etc., up to 'we change enemies into friends by the sacrifice of intention.' Crying out, they wept. Because the stroke had changed the appearance of the stricken man, a spontaneous grief changes the appearance of the consolers: because one who does not share the grief but clings and drags cannot console the grieving. Therefore, seeing the body torn, they tear their garments; seeing it changed, they defile their heads with dust, that Job may more readily listen to them while he sees something of his own affliction in them. Yet the consoler must see to it that he does not, by grieving too much, burden the afflicted and make the grieving despair: perhaps Job's friends grieved too much, not knowing the mind of the stricken man, as though he had fallen from the heart. They sprinkled dust. Dust is earthly understanding; the head is the mind; heaven is the precept of supernal speech. To cast dust upon the head toward heaven is to corrupt the mind with worldly understanding, and to think earthly things from heavenly words. Day is understanding, night ignorance, seven the totality. They sit, then, that is, they pretend to condescend to the weakness of the Church, both in those matters in which they understand the true light and in those in which they have ignorance, and so they prepare the snares of deception.
2.13: 2.13 On the ground. Because they show an appearance of humility in order to persuade proud things. Or the ground is the incarnation of Christ, which certain heretics do not deny, but differ from us either about the divinity or about the quality of the incarnation: so, since they do not deny it, they sit with Job on the ground, as it were. Seven days. It is not known whether continuously, or whether they persisted for so many days by frequent visits. Days and nights. Because whether in what they think rightly or in what they think foolishly, they do not contradict the incarnation. None spoke a word to him. Because enemies are silent then, if we neglect to beget sons of God by preaching; but if we speak rightly, then they heap on grave insults, and burst out against us in a voice of pain. The seeds of errors do speak when they see the hearts of the faithful grow numb; but when they see them savor high things, grieve over the hardship of the world, and seek the return to heaven, they curb their tongue with caution. None spoke. For there are many, etc., up to 'and unless they are purged by sacrifice, they are to be punished.' For they saw his grief. Because they fear to speak perverse things then, when the grief of the love of God shapes hearts: for they would not then make progress, but would lose even those they held, through the good that had been practiced.
3.1: 3.1 After this, etc. He makes the hearers attentive, as to hidden things that were covered in closed vessels, but are uncovered when their mouth is opened, so that we may be refreshed by their inmost fragrance. Thus far a threefold exposition; from here as each passage requires. Gregory. He cursed his day. Behold, this is not according to the surface of the history, for it is both evil and impossible. For the day on which he was born no longer existed, and it is idle to curse a thing that does not exist, and harmful if it did exist; nor can a past day be turned into darkness, nor can the other things that follow suit it, nor would a stillborn child, as he says afterward, enjoy rest; therefore here nothing is according to the letter. After this. That is, after all the things said before, which he suffered, his friends also being silent. Since, then, he gave thanks patiently in everything and taught well, he is not now to be believed to burst out into cursing from impatience, with nobody instigating, but he says this in quiet, because amid evils he praised God. He cursed. Same place. 'Curse' is said in two ways, etc., up to 'and applies the remedy.'
3.3: 3.3 Let the day perish on which I was born. Not created, etc., up to 'but he brought in the darkness of sin.' Let the day perish. The day is the prosperity of the world, which ends in night, because it leads to tribulation; or the day is the delight of sin, the night the blindness of the mind. 'Man' is said in three ways: by nature, by guilt, and by weakness. Man, then, is born in the day and conceived in the night: because he is not carried off to the delight of sin unless he is first weakened through the darkness of the mind. But let the day perish, that is, let the delight of sin be destroyed by the vigor of justice. And the night. Gregory, on Job, book 4. That is, let repentance extinguish what the blinded mind carries out by consent, while it does not carefully see the allurements of delight, lest the guilt that begins to flatter drag it to destruction.
3.4: 3.4 Let that day, etc. Same place. That is, from the beginning of delight, let it be seen to what end of perdition it hurries, and let it be tormented through repentance. But if it is so punished. Let God not seek it. In judgment, that he may punish; and let light not shine upon it. He who accuses illumines with light; but he is as it were covered who is not recalled to the memory of the judge. Hence: 'Blessed are they whose sins are covered' (Psalm 31); and then they will not be shown in the sight of all.
3.5: 3.5 Let light not shine upon it, etc. Let darkness obscure it. That is, the day of delight, lest it be seen by him who sees all things. Darkness. Gregory. That is, the lamentations of repentance or the hidden judgments of God, from which we are absolved by prevenient grace, which we do not know how to deserve. And the shadow of death. That is, the death of Christ according to the flesh, etc., up to 'in which mercy comes to help, let man punish this': hence follows: Let a mist take hold of it. That is, confusion of mind, of which it is said: 'For there is a confusion that brings glory' (Sirach 4). And let it be wrapped round. On every side. With bitterness. Of repentance; but if the day, that is, the delight of sin, is so punished, what of the night, that is, consent to guilt?
3.6: 3.6 Let a tempestuous whirlwind seize that night. As though a whirlwind of the storm were stirred up, etc., up to 'for the blindness of damnation in which we were born.' Let it not be counted in the days of the year. The year is the grace from above, etc., up to 'but it is forever without share in that homeland.' Hence he adds:
3.7: 3.7 Let that night be solitary. Because it is separated from that company, or loses the man whom it had made its companion; and with the elect redeemed by grace, it is handed over alone with its body to Gehenna. Nor worthy of praise. When man was cast down, he worshiped idols, in which he praised demons as though the darkness of night; but now that the idols are rejected, the night is worthy of praise.
3.8: 3.8 Let them curse it. Same place. In the old translation, etc., up to 'and at the end, set loose, let him openly wage wars.' Leviathan. That is, their addition, that is, of men, in whom after the suggestion he does not cease to add evils. Or reproach, because when he promised to add divinity to Adam, he took away what he had. He is called by the prophet the twisting serpent, who softly pours in ambushes, as it were with the flattering ends of words. And the bar, because he is hard through malice and strikes to kill. When stirred up he will act openly, but meanwhile secretly.
3.9: 3.9 By the darkness of that night. Let the stars be darkened. That is, the hypocrites, who shine through works before the eyes of men. These are the ones drawn by the tail of the dragon, that is, by the final persecution of Antichrist; these are darkened, because the enemy's malice so prevails over them that they are wrapped in open evils, such within as they are without. Let it look for light. This is according to his members, etc., up to 'which endured Christ by prophesying, but did not recognize him when he came.' Nor the rising of the dawn. Same place. The rising of the dawn is the new birth of the resurrection, by which the saints will arise with the flesh to see the eternal light. But however brightly the elect shine here, they cannot penetrate what that glory of the new birth will be: this night did not shut, but opened, the doors of the womb, because, man being conceived, it unlocked the desires of concupiscence toward sin. But when these doors, that is, the desires of carnal concupiscence, are unlocked, we are drawn into the countless evils of corruption. Hence, burdened, we groan: because justice requires that what we did willingly we bear unwillingly.
3.10: 3.10 Because it did not shut the doors of the womb, etc. This is of the head itself, etc., up to 'as we say that robbers give life to their captives, if they do not take it away.'
3.11: 3.11 Why did I not die in the womb? It is not to be believed, etc., up to 'lest the suggestion draw to delight.' And come forth from the womb. Gregory. Because sin conceived is outwardly, etc., up to 'while they bear the contention of their own flesh against the spirit.'
3.13: 3.13 For now. Same place. By 'now,' which is of the present time, he designates the eternal rest, which always stands in the present. I would have rested with kings. That is, the angels, because they rule the things subject to them. Who are also counselors, because by announcing the will of God they counsel us. Or he calls the holy preachers kings, because they rule themselves, and counselors of the earth, because they counsel earthly men well. He says, then, that if he had not sinned, he would have ascended there even unredeemed, to which the apostles and holy preachers come after redemption with great labor, who are not delayed as the ancients were, but enter heaven soon after death. Who build. Every earthly man is pressed in his heart by dense tumults of thoughts, and trampled by the throng of desires as by crowds. But to build solitudes is to drive out the tumults of earthly desires from the secret of the heart and to pant for the love of inner quiet, so that he can say: 'One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek,' etc.
3.15: 3.15 With princes who possess gold. The princes are the rulers of the Church, etc., up to 'but he who foresaw the future already recalls the past.'
3.16: 3.16 Or as an untimely birth. Same place. Because what is untimely is born before its time and, extinguished, is straightway hidden. These are the saints with whom he considers he could have rested, who were from the beginning of the world before the time of redemption, and yet mortified themselves to the world. The first time, before the law, which brought forth the fathers dead a second time, was like the womb of an untimely birth; and they themselves died, as it were, from the womb, who without the tables of the law feared God naturally and, believing in the future redeemer, put pleasures to death. Hidden. Because, with few mentioned by Moses, etc., up to 'on whom the spirit of prophecy shone, like Job himself.' Same place. He now opens the rest of this light, and shows in plainer words what is done daily near it regarding the conduct of the impious.
3.17: 3.17 There the wicked. That is, in the light of Christ, which the ancients awaited, the Gentiles cease from the crowd of the world's desires and with a tranquil mind already taste beforehand the eternal rest. And this is: And there they rested. In the world the strong in power are said not to be weary. But he who is strengthened in the love of God fails salutarily from his own strength, and the more strongly he seeks the eternal, the more wearied he dies in earthly things. Hence: 'My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord' (Psalm 38). When he says 'there' of the light, he shows the place of the elect in which they are contained.
3.18: 3.18 And once bound. The just, though quiet from desires, while yet in the body are bound by the trouble of their corruption. For the body weighs down the soul, and the flesh strives against the spirit. There are also bodily chains, hunger, thirst and the like, which cannot be loosed here; but they will be loosed from all in the freedom of the glory of the sons of God. See the stages: the converted wicked cease; the exercised rest in the inmost bosom; released from the chains of corruption they come to freedom. But what they did here meanwhile he adds: They did not hear, etc. The taskmaster is the devil, who once laid on man the coin of deception and daily exacts the debt of death; his voice is temptation. He hears who is tempted and resists; he gives ear who consents. The same of inner peace, because what the mind loves greatly it repeats more often.
3.19: 3.19 Small and great are there. Same place. Because here is the distinction of works, there will be that of dignities. Hence: 'In my Father's house there are many mansions' (John 14). And the servant. He who sins is a servant of sin, because here he never becomes free while he fears the judge; but there he will be free, where there will be no doubt about pardon. There will indeed be there a memory of guilt, not one that pollutes the mind, but one that, without harm to blessedness, binds it more closely to blessedness and joy, so that, healed, we remember our pains without pain; hence we give the physician greater thanks.
3.20: 3.20 Why is light given to the wretched? Gregory, on Job, book 5. Having contemplated rest, where, free in the Lord, he looks down on the prosperity of the world, which draws back from it. Why is light given to the wretched, that is, prosperity in the misery of the pilgrimage: because, if it does not wholly oppress the just man, it nevertheless divides the mind between the love of God and the management of itself; hence he adds: And life to those who, etc. There is bitterness for every just man, etc., up to 'or to preside in government.'
3.21: 3.21 Who wait for death. Same place. That is, they desire to mortify themselves wholly to the world, but by the hidden judgment of God it does not come, because they are compelled to be occupied with imposed offices, which they bear from the fear of God; and within there is the desire of piety, and outwardly they fulfil the duty of their rank, lest through pride they contradict God's disposition; and so they both profit many, and by seeing themselves imperfect they rise higher through humility; and that they are put off from their desires, by that very delay they are enlarged toward the same; hence he adds, as it were digging, etc. As it were digging for a treasure. For he who seeks a treasure by digging, etc., up to 'finds examples of contemplation, whence he may be rich.'
3.22: 3.22 To a man whose. Behold, when it was asked why light is given to the wretched, he shows here: his way is hidden from the man; for if he now does well, he does not know what he will do at the end; or at times what is thought to please God displeases.
3.23: 3.23 God has surrounded him. Gregory. Because although he desires heavenly things, yet he does not know what is disposed for him within. There is also around him the darkness of ignorance: he is forgetful of the past, does not find out the future, scarcely knows the present, and cannot penetrate the inmost dispensation of God. But he who attends to this darkness weeps, and with all his sight seeks the light above; hence it sometimes happens that in pious weeping the brightness of inner joy bursts forth; hence follows:
3.24: 3.24 Before I eat. To eat is to be fed by the light of contemplation, which he has not who has not first, in this exile, groaned as in a place where there are no goods, and sighed with desire and carried out the force of tears. And like overflowing waters, etc. Overflowing waters are carried by the force of many billows; so in the mourning there are many billows, since they do not know what will be decreed for them with God: while they recall their past they fear the future, and in their good deeds they dread going astray; and when the scourges of God correct them they suspect they have offended; hence he adds:
3.25: 3.25 For the fear. They weep because they fear to be forsaken, and lest the pious stroke be not of discipline but of vengeance; hence: 'Who knows the power of your anger?' (Psalm 89). For sometimes what we call anger is grace, and sometimes what we call grace is anger, hence it is necessary that in all things there be fear: in prosperity, lest it be given to them for greater blinding and not for consolation, as is usual with the good; lest in adversity there be the beginning of punishment.
3.26: 3.26 Have I not dissembled? Same place. And if always thinking, etc., up to 'if Job sets forth as an example what he was in power.' Have I not dissembled? Power held is to be considered also for usefulness, and to be dissembled on account of pride, and the powerful man should know that he can be of benefit. Have I not been silent? Behold what he is in speech. Have I not been quiet? Behold what he is toward unlawful things, etc., up to 'because our perfection is not without fault'; hence he adds: And indignation has come upon me. Hence, about to speak of the blows with great art, he put first his right deeds, so that in these each might consider what punishment awaits the wicked, if it so chastises the just here, that if the just man will scarcely be saved, where will the ungodly appear?
4.2: 4.2 If we begin to speak to you. Same place. They begin gently, but burst into harsh words. So heretics set forth smooth words, lest they be guarded against, but subjoin harsh ones. But the conceived. Same place. The perfect do not even conceive perverse things in the heart, which they restrain in silence. Others conceive perverse things but restrain them with great strength of silence; others both conceive and soon bring them forth. Light in mind, hasty in tongue. Of these is Eliphaz, who by his own experience thinks the same of all. Who can withhold? As if he wanted to hold back: in which he hints that he will give offense in speaking.
4.3: 4.3 Behold, you have taught many. Same place. These are certain goods, which even he confesses who wishes to accuse. How great he was before, who, occupied with disposing so many of his own affairs, freely taught others as well, showing right things in deed and word. But because the accuser says good things of him, he turned to a charge, saying:
4.5: 4.5 But now it has come, etc., as if you did not keep the right things you were saying. Note, however, that there are wicked men who say the goods of the just which they cannot deny are known, lest they seem perverse; and so that they may be the more believed in the evils they insert, they turn even these very goods into a heaping up of guilt. Here, then, he says that Job spoke rightly but did not keep it, so that the evil man is reproved by his own testimony; below he is charged with speaking badly, so that he may be silent. And these are the two ways in which the wicked assail the good, saying that they either say perverse things or do not hold the good things they say. You have failed, etc. Where is your fear? As if he marvels at the lost virtues, which he places in fitting order. As on the way of the world boldness begets strength and fear weakness, so on the way of God boldness begets weakness and the fear of God strength; for he who is joined to God is lifted by a certain power above all things; strength is shown only in adversities, hence patience is added, because he makes progress in strength who bears others' evils unmoved. From patience perfection is born, hence man is said to possess his soul in patience, that is, to live rightly in all things, to rule all the movements of the mind by virtue: for he who conquers himself is strong against everything. Same place. But since he rebuked by inveighing, he now adds as if by exhorting:
4.7: 4.7 Remember, I beg you. But this too he does reprehensibly. For the innocent and upright are often wholly destroyed here, though they are kept for eternal things; but those who serve God not for the eternal but for an earthly reward invent for themselves what they seek, and presuming to teach, when they preach earthly security they show by all their labors what they love.
4.8: 4.8 But rather I have seen them. Same place. He sows sorrows who speaks; he reaps deceitful things who prevails by speaking. Or he sows sorrows who does perverse things; he reaps who prospers in them. These do not perish as he says, but live here more happily than the just. For God allows some to prevail here, that the life of the just may be purged the more cleanly. Others he punishes at once, lest he be thought to neglect human things and to pass over many evils, in order to strengthen the hearts of the innocent who are fainthearted; yet he would speak more truly of all at the end; it could generally be said that the innocent and upright does not perish, because even if he is ground down here, he is restored with God to true salvation. And the wicked perish, because even if they grow higher here, at the end they will be struck the harder. But because he says 'remember,' it is clear that past things are being recalled to mind, not future things announced.
4.9: 4.9 Perished by the blast of God. Same place. We blow air as we draw it from outside in and return it from inside out. God is therefore said to blow in retribution, because from outward causes he conceives within the counsel of judgment, and from the inner counsel he sends forth the sentence outwardly, that is, from our evils which he sees outside he disposes judgment within, and from the inner conception he makes damnation outside. Or God is said to blow, that is, to be angry, by comparison, because we, when angry, are inflamed by a breath of fury. God therefore blows in anger, thinking vengeance, when, after long patience, he who is tranquil in himself seems turbulent to the guilty, when they themselves are troubled before him by their guilt. Gregory. After he gently admonished, he openly rebukes. The roaring of the lion, that is, the severity and terror of Job himself; the voice of the lioness, the talkativeness of his wife; the teeth of the whelps, the greediness of his sons, has been destroyed. Rigid, he exults, as if they had been condemned by right. He also compares Job to the tigress for the spots of pretense. For the hypocrite, who seems upright, has hidden vices, which sometimes breaking out change his color. The prey is the glory of the just, which he seizes for himself: thinking therefore that holy Job had held the goods he knew in him through hypocrisy, he says:
4.11: 4.11 The tigress has perished. That is, the variety of your pretense has been extinguished, etc., up to 'such men think by wisdom to transcend all.'
4.12: 4.12 Now a hidden word was spoken to me. Same place. Heretics pretend to hear hidden things, hence they preach secretly, so that their preaching may be held more holy, not equal to that of others. Stealthily, etc. Same place. Because they do not enter with the others by the door but seek the chinks of a perverse understanding; and because the thief fears the light, he adds:
4.13: 4.13 In the horror of a night vision. They say they have perceived the veins of the divine whisper in the dread of a night vision, because to boast of lofty things they say they can scarcely grasp them. But while they thus mark them as lofty, they are witnesses of wickedness against themselves. For in a night vision one sees doubtfully. When sleep is wont to take hold. That is, while all below sleep in torpor, we wake to perceive high and heavenly things. And when they sometimes see this despised, they pretend to fear what they say, hence he adds:
4.14: 4.14 Fear took hold of me. So that they may seem wondrous in lofty things, they pretend to be afraid of what they invent; and yet they are bold to bring forth what they assert they could scarcely hear. A word was spoken to me. Same place. The Son of God is said, etc., up to 'so much the more, being restrained, it dreads his uprightness'; hence he adds: In the horror of a night vision, etc. That is, in the dread of hidden contemplation, in which nothing is seen plainly, but as if in image. But no one reaches this unless carnal desires are repressed, hence: When sleep is wont to take hold of men. He wakes who attends to the cares of the world; he sleeps in quiet who flees them. This is Jacob, who sleeps on the journey and sees angels, that is, in the course of this life closes his eyes to worldly things, which guilt opened to the first parents for coveting. And no one is led to see inner things unless he is withdrawn from what entangles him outwardly; hence: 'Be still and see that I am God' (Psalm 45). But the higher the mind is lifted in contemplation and sees things above itself, the more fearfully it trembles within itself, hence: Fear took hold of me and trembling and all my bones. Same place. That is, the stronger acts, etc., up to 'feels the sting of the flesh,' he adds:
4.16: 4.16 One stood. Same place. That they may judge themselves to know incomprehensible things, etc., up to 'because he specially arrogated to himself a common good.' The hair of my flesh stood up. Same place. Hairs are any superfluous things of human corruption, the thoughts of the old life; if we shut them out of the mind, we cut the hairs from the flesh, so that we are not wearied by pain. Hence Moses: 'Let the Levites shave all the hair of their flesh' (Leviticus 14). We see these more subtly in ourselves when we penetrate lofty things, hence it is rightly said now: When a spirit passed by. For when the mind sees true things, it torments itself the more harshly over superfluities. As the spirit passes, therefore, the hairs are afraid, because superfluous thoughts flee before the force of compunction, because the inner vision inflames the soul against itself; and while it strictly cuts away unlawful things, the mind clings more broadly to contemplation, and well fixes the spirit that was passing by, and yet this very delay of contemplation does not fully open the power of piety, hence he adds: One stood whose face I did not know. Same place. 'A certain one' is not said, etc., up to 'he beholds through his coeternal appearance,' he adds: An image before my eyes. The image of the Father is the Son, who says: 'No one comes to the Father but by me.' And I heard a voice as of a gentle breeze. Same place. The voice of the breeze is knowledge, etc., up to 'who learned from this hearing.'
4.17: 4.17 Shall man be justified in comparison with God? He knew this in contemplation, that human justice compared with divine is injustice, so that a lamp that shines in darkness grows dim in the sun: which he could, because he who sees the light knows what to think of the darkness. Or purer than his maker? Same place. He thinks this who murmurs against the one who scourges. But he ought to know that he who made wonders out of nothing does not scourge impiously, and the founder of nature is not an unjust judge of guilt. Although this man unjustly rebukes Job, he rightly describes the measure of the creature in comparison with the Creator. A man thinks himself purer than his maker if he prepares a complaint against the scourge, and without doubt puts him below himself when he rebukes his judgment on his affliction. Behold, those who serve him. The same. An angel, although he remains unchangeable in his state, yet in that he is a creature has the vicissitude of mutability, and so is not stable. For if this nature were not changeable, being well made it would have fallen in none. But by choice it had to fall or stand, and in those who stood it was merit that by the zeal of will they fixed the motion of their mutability. This is the proof of mutability, which he adds of the apostate: And in his angels he found wickedness. From comparison with these human weakness is gathered. How much more those who dwell in houses of clay. Gregory. That is, earthly bodies, etc., up to 'they behold, occupied with the cares of the world'; hence he adds:
4.20: 4.20 From morning till evening. That is, from the beginning of their life to its end they are wounded by the commission of iniquity, by which, cut off, they fall into the depth. Same place. Or morning is prosperity, evening adversity; but through both they perish, because through prosperity they are wanton, through adversity impatient, and rise to madness. And because none of them, namely those who are cut down from morning till evening, understands what is kept here for the afflicted good, what is to be for themselves who think good things here. But because not all are so abandoned, he adds: But those who shall be left. That is, the despised of the world, whom the world has left as unworthy, as the Egyptian boy, that is, the lover of the world, black with sins, often despised by the world is left behind, so that he does not run with it, but, broken by adversities, lies numb. But David, that is, Christ, finds him, and turns him to his love, and feeds him with the food of the word, and makes him the guide of the journey, that is, his preacher; and under that guidance he destroys those feasting, that is, the joy of the world, which despised having him as a companion. They shall be taken away from them. Because God chose them for himself. They shall die, and not in wisdom. The lot of the just being interposed, he returns to the ruin of those without understanding. The reprobate despise the just, because through their death they seek the invisible, or through death seek the invisible life. But those who alike flee death and wisdom wholly forsake wisdom, unwilling to die for the truth, yet do not escape death.
5.1: 5.1 Call now. Same place. Because he truly brought this forward against the wicked, although he secretly placed Job among their number: puffed up by the pride of wisdom, he adds open mockery against Job: Call now, that is, if you cry out afflicted, God does not answer, that is, gives no effect, because in tranquillity you despised him; and to which of the saints, that is, you have no holy helpers in affliction, because you had no companions in gladness. Same place. After the mockery he adds a sentence, etc., up to 'this troubles the wise, but anger through vice slays fools.' And it kills the little one. That is, while he envies one whom he thinks greater, etc., up to 'or by having a part limits the quantity for us.' Gregory, Morals book 6, chapter 5. Because with all desires he is fixed in earthly love, hence Cain first built a city on the earth, a stranger to heaven, who lives here more happily.
5.3: 5.3 And I cursed his beauty. The same. Because, although from the seen prosperity of the wicked the feet of the weak totter, the strong, seeing what punishment follows their glory, at once reject their prosperity. The weak man changes with the quality of things; when he sees prosperity he praises, when it changes he judges it nothing; but the firm man, with the glory itself, considers the punishment that follows, and at once condemns it. But because those who advance in the world draw many with them, he adds:
5.4: 5.4 His sons shall be far off. That is, his followers. In the gate. Same place. The gate of the kingdom is the day of judgment, in which the elect enter into glory; before it the sons of this world are exalted, but then they shall be crushed.
5.5: 5.5 And there shall be none to deliver. Same place. Because truth snatches those there whom discipline presses here. Whose harvest. Each one has the gift of understanding, by which he understands and says what is right; but because he neither loves nor does the same, he fasts from the harvest he has; but he who hungers for justice, hearing right things from him, refreshes himself, hence: 'What they say, do' (Matthew 23). And the armed man shall seize him. Same place. The devil is overcome as unarmed when, suggesting open evils, he tries to take away all goods alike; but armed he conquers, passing over some goods untouched, secretly corrupting others. And they shall drink. The same. A fool often has riches, etc., up to 'and the studious is hindered by slowness?' he answers:
5.6: 5.6 Nothing upon earth is done without a cause. Because from this the one is more justly punished for negligence, the other crowned for diligence. But because we are taught to understand right things not only by study but also by persecutions, it is added: And out of the ground sorrow does not spring. And out of the ground sorrow does not spring. Same place. The ground, that is, the elements of the world, are turned to the punishment of wrongdoers; hence it is said: 'The whole world will fight for him,' that is, for the Lord, 'against the senseless'; yet sorrow does not come forth from them, because punishment is not born from the things that strike, but from those who by sinning have extorted the blows; but the more the outward punishment chastises, the more the mind is raised to heavenly things; hence he adds:
5.7: 5.7 Man is born to labor. Because it is impossible to be without labor in this pilgrimage; but in that the flesh is afflicted, the mind is raised to seek lofty things. Or 'man,' that is, the carnal man, feels the evils of the world because he greedily seeks its goods. But he whose mind passes beyond these things, like a bird to the heights, lifted by the wing of hope, feels no evil, and rejoices even in scourges; but because no one can do this by his own strength, he adds:
5.8: 5.8 Wherefore I will beseech you. That is, I ask him through whom I know these things are bestowed.
5.9: 5.9 Wonders without number. Because the greatness of the divine works can neither be examined by quality nor numbered by quantity.
5.10: 5.10 Who gives rain. Same place. These words are mystical, because Job's friends had been instructed by his company. He gives rain upon the earth: when he pours the grace of preaching on the dry hearts of the Gentiles. And waters all things with waters. When he fills man with the Spirit for bearing fruit. Man is called 'all things,' because he has something in common with all things. Or 'all things,' that is, the rich and the poor, and all the differences of men, because retribution follows a good work.
5.11: 5.11 Who sets up the lowly on high. Gregory. So that those now despised may judge with the Lord. The mourners. Because the more they are now troubled by adversities and chasten themselves by lamentations, the more exalted safety they will have even in this life. This can be understood of the elect, where the humble with lofty mind transcend all temporal things, and the afflicted are lifted up in safety, not in madness, like those who rejoice when they have done evil. These rejoice from the certainty of eternal salvation.
5.12: 5.12 Who scatters the thoughts. The same. Although the reprobate think evil, God sometimes takes away their strength, lest they prevail against the good, so that they lack the effect of the deed, and before God are guilty in conscience.
5.13: 5.13 Who catches the wise. Same place. Because human acts serve the counsels of God fittingly even when they resist, as in the selling of Joseph, so that he would not be worshiped; in Saul's demand for the foreskins, so that David might be destroyed; in the death of the Lord, so that not all would believe in him. God grants some things propitiously, permits others in anger; and these he then turns to the use of his counsel, so that what opposes his counsel fights for his counsel, and what is done without his will is not contrary to his will, hence: 'All things whatsoever he willed,' etc.
5.14: 5.14 In the day they shall meet with darkness. Because in the very presence of truth they are blinded by the error of unfaithfulness, seeing the miracles of Christ and doubting his divinity. As in the night. We seek by groping what we do not see with our eyes: the Jews had seen the miracles and still sought as though groping: 'If you are the Christ, tell us plainly' (John 10). But Christ could not be held long by their hands. In the day they shall meet with darkness. Same place. The mind of the envious man, when afflicted by another's good, is darkened by the ray of the sun. And they shall grope at noonday as in the night. The day of good work shines outwardly in the neighbor; they grope as in the night, because, blinded by spite, they busy themselves to find something to reprehend. Behold Lot, that is, the just man, when the wicked oppose, is shut up and protected within the house, that is, returns to the mind and remains within; the Sodomites, blind, go round about, that is, the envious scrutinize deeds and words, and do not find the door, that is, an entrance for reproach, but grope the wall, because the praiseworthy action of the just meets them everywhere. They shall grope. But the poor in spirit, that is, one who is not exalted in himself, is saved from the sword of the mouth, that is, from wicked persuasion.
5.15: 5.15 But he shall save the needy from the sword of their mouth. The sword of the mouth is the accusation of the Jews. The hand of the violent is the Gentile world which crucified; but Christ overcame these by rising again. In this needy one, that is, the humble people of the faithful, the hope of the life to come is made firm. And iniquity, which now opens its mouth in insult to Christ, will shut it through punishment, or being converted ceases from injuries. The same generally of the perverse. The poor from the hand of the violent. That is, from an adverse power, so that he is neither drawn by the allurements of persuasions nor broken by the pain of torments. The poor man is not drawn, because his hope, fixed on eternal things, is made firm against these. When the poor man has come to the fruit of that hope, the exalted one falls silent and draws in his mouth: because torments bind the tongue that spoke against the just by detracting. But for the elect to escape punishments and reach the rewards, he must be purged here by scourges, hence he adds:
5.17: 5.17 Do not therefore reject the chastening of the Lord. Same place. He rejects it who complains that he suffers unjustly. Eliphaz, then, thinking Job is struck for purification and not for the proving of his strength, because Job speaks freely, seeking the causes of his stroke, thinks he rejects the chastening of the Lord. So heretics turn what is rightly done by the Church to evil.
5.18: 5.18 For he wounds. The same. God wounds in two ways those whom he brings back to salvation. Sometimes he strikes in the body to heal the mind; sometimes without outward scourges he strikes the hardness of the mind with his own desire, and thus heals that which was lying dead in security in the world. But while the mind pants for God and despises all worldly things, all things are soon turned into temptation for it and afflict it; but while it is worn down by transitory labor, it is freed from the perpetual, and therefore he adds:
5.19: 5.19 In six troubles. Same place. By the six, which a seventh follows, the working and course of the present life is signified: because on the sixth day God, finishing all things, made man, and rested on the seventh, which has no evening, that is, no end; in the seventh trouble, therefore, he delivers, lest evil touch him in the seventh: because here he wears us down by teaching as a father, but on the day of judgment he hides us from the lash.
5.20: 5.20 In famine. Same place. He enumerates the evils of the present life and the helps of God. The famine of the mind is the silence of the word of God: when this is withdrawn, the temptation of the flesh, which is war, grows strong. But God even in famine rescues the soul from death, because he refreshes it with his word. And in war. He makes us strong against the temptations of the flesh. But one made such sometimes fears detractions, hence he adds:
5.21: 5.21 From the scourge of the tongue. That is, from the reproach of insult, on account of which, mocked, one ceases from good; hence David: 'And from the harsh word.' From this the saint is hidden, because, while he seeks no praise here, he does not feel insults either; but because after these one fears some torment of bodies, there follows: And you shall not fear calamity. That is, of persecution; but because such a one prepares for himself security against the terror of the judgment to come, he adds:
5.22: 5.22 In destruction and famine. Destruction is Gehenna, which is outside, etc., up to 'so that at the point of his death the assault does not terrify,' there is added: And the beasts of the earth. Which at the time of death are unleashed to seize souls, but he does not fear them raging, who did not follow them when flattering; and the beginning of retribution is security of mind at death. But when one lives well, he must take care that, despising the rest, he not glory in being singular, but think of the common good, hence he adds:
5.23: 5.23 But you shall have a covenant with the stones of the regions. As though the regions of the nations are divided, differing in the Church's customs and tongues; the stones are the elect, who are placed in the building. He who lives rightly, therefore, joins himself to the stones by covenant: because in that he forsakes the world, he binds himself to the saints by imitation; hence the assault increases, yet ground down by it he is more humbly subject to God, hence he adds: And the beasts of the earth. Not pacified but peacemakers, because they do not have peace but make peace; because when a man is more sharply assailed by the devil, he is driven the more to love, and with him peace is made firmer. Or the beasts are the movements of the flesh, which, pressed as in a cage by continence, though they roar in tempting, do not pass to the effect, as to the rage of a bite, in which they are peaceable. Or because they trouble, that state in which one lives without contradiction is the more loved; and so they drive us to the love of inner quiet.
5.24: 5.24 And you shall know that your tent has peace. Gregory. Peace is either begun, which is conceived here from the desire of God, or full, which comes in the future from the vision of God. When, then, the mind is subjected to God, or the flesh to the mind, the tabernacle of the just man, that is, the body which the mind inhabits, has peace, the movements of desires being restrained under justice. But this chastity of the flesh is nothing if the sweetness of the mind in love of neighbor is lacking. And visiting your beauty you shall not sin. Same place. Our beauty is the neighbor, etc., up to 'because from the seed of good work he gathers abundant fruits of preaching'; hence it is added:
5.25: 5.25 You shall know also that your seed shall be multiplied. For he receives the eloquence of speaking well who lives well, and whose conscience does not hinder the speaker. Hence the Egyptians, made slaves, receive grain for seed, who before, being free, had received it for food: because when we are fully subject to God, we are filled with the word of preaching. Before, being free, they were fed on sacred speech, and yet were at leisure for certain things which we seek in the world. From preaching a great offspring of the faithful follows. And this is: And your offspring like the grass of the earth. That is, innumerable. Or he is compared to grass because, forsaking the withering glory of the world, he grows green by inner hope. But it is not enough for the just man to do these great things outwardly unless he also penetrates through contemplation into eternal things; hence it is added:
5.26: 5.26 You shall enter the sepulcher in abundance. Same place. The sepulcher is contemplation, etc., up to 'that they pour back for the benefit of neighbors.' As a heap of wheat is brought in. Because the time of action comes first, the last is that of contemplation. And it is necessary that the perfect man first exercise his mind in the virtues, and afterward store it in the granary of rest. Or the sepulcher is eternal rest, in which one rests the more truly the more perfectly the life of corruption is put to death. He enters it in abundance who, after the works of this life have been heaped up, fully dead to this mutability, is hidden in the secret of the true light, like wheat: because the just feel blows in a time not their own, but in their own they enter the granary like grains.
5.27: 5.27 We have searched it out. In this he marks that he did not speak according to the surface above of the sepulcher, the beasts, the stones, the tabernacle, and the like, but sought inner things in them. Which, having heard, ponder in your mind. Words of boasting; and even if he taught well, it is lack of skill to wish to teach a better man: hence the sayings of the friends, though right, are charged with not being rightly said.
6.2: 6.2 Oh that my sins were weighed. Touched by scourges, he is provoked by words, not so as to fall stubborn, lifted up to a defense, but as one who, struck, silently gave thanks and, provoked, replied rightly: Oh that my sins were weighed. The balance. Same place. Christ, in the hand of the Father, holding the scale of mercy and justice, shows sin, relaxed by mercy, to be light, and the calamity, by dying, to be of heavy weight. To him he also gives this of grace, that the calamity itself may be known. For blind man rejoiced in exile as in his homeland; but God, appearing outside, calls man back within, so that, having seen what he lost, he grieves heavily for what he endures. He says therefore: Oh that they were weighed. That is, the evil of our, etc., up to 'weighing the judgments of God by which he is afflicted,' and this is:
6.3: 6.3 Hence my words also are full of sorrow, for the arrows of the Lord. That is, the stroke of God's chastisement, which does not leave me, as it does many, unpurified.
6.4: 6.4 Drinks up my spirit. Gregory. That is, it restrains elation, so that he may say: 'My spirit has failed' (Psalm 76). And not only do I groan at what I suffer, but I fear what you threaten, and this is: The terrors of the Lord war against me: lest eternal death follow after this. But because he desires the coming of the stature, with what ardor the Gentile world and Judea thirst for the same, he supplies when he says:
6.5: 6.5 Will the wild ass bray, that is, the rustic ass, etc., up to 'but he was held carnally,' he adds:
6.6: 6.6 Or can that which is unsavory be eaten? Salt is the power of hidden understanding, etc., up to 'by turning, hungering, he received.' Same place. He desires the balance, we already live by faith in him; but yet for purification we suffer his arrows, and fear from the terror of the future. But because we are sons, we ought not to fear as of a Lord, but to love as a Father, and to pant for him, where we shall be fed with food, that is, his eternity, for which we now bray, hence: Will the wild ass bray? Same place. The wild ass is the people which, etc., up to 'also separate themselves from words of this kind,' and this is: Or can that which is unsavory be eaten? But now placed on high, removed from fools, often, while they provide only for their own bearing of hard things, they are not girded for the love of truth. Or can anyone taste. Gregory. It is hard to seek what tortures, what drives away life, but often, when one is on high, he stoops to bear the evils of fools, to draw them. For with the desire for heavenly things increased, he is hemmed in, and for the sweetness of those things does not fear the bitter things of the world. Hence, also, after the impossible taste of death, he adds:
6.7: 6.7 What before he refused to touch, that is, the evils of the world, are now sweet foods because of the love of heaven. And since these are sweet: Who will grant that my petition may come?
6.9: 6.9 May he who began crush me. Gregory, on Job, book 7. The adversary crushes, and man fails from you. God crushes, and one broken by vices is made firm in virtue. He who desires, then, to draw near to God through scourges says: May he who began crush, because sometimes God begins the crushing of vices, and man, advanced at that very beginning, is lifted up, and so the enemy, shut out, returns more grievous with other spirits taken in, and crushes virtues. Let him loose his hand, that is, let him exercise the effect; for when one, puffed up by long prosperity, does not exercise his love through scourges, he holds his hand bound, as it were, from striking vices, hence he says to the sinning people: 'I will no longer be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you.' Let him cut me off. For when sorrow or temptation does not strike, the elation of the mind, cut down, falls, so that it now seeks the hand of the one lifting.
6.10: 6.10 And let this be my consolation, that afflicting me. Same place. As if he spares some here in order to strike eternally; but let him not spare me here but strike, which is my consolation. For the saints fear to be spared here. That he said this not with a swelling but with a humble mind, he shows in what follows. Nor will I contradict the words. The words of God to us are not only sayings but also deeds, such as here the stroke upon Job; against which by murmuring he does not contradict, because he also calls holy him whom he endures in striking.
6.11: 6.11 For what is my strength? Same place. The strength of the good is one thing, etc., up to 'and refuses to suffer for the one he does not love'; he says therefore: For what is my strength, or what is my end? That is, evils, etc., up to 'whence the weak has strength,' hence he adds:
6.13: 6.13 Behold, there is no help. To the greater merit of strength, how he is forsaken by those close to him, he adds: Even those necessary. If despised outwardly, within he presides on the throne of judgment; for he bursts into sentences: He who takes away, etc.
6.14: 6.14 He who takes away from his friend. Same place. A friend is any neighbor, etc., up to 'who within have long since perished by neglecting eternal things'; of whom it is rightly said:
6.17: 6.17 And when they grow warm, that is, when through the knowledge of punishment they begin to burn, they shall be separated from the delight of the flesh which they held by desire. The wicked do not understand eternal things unless when they are already punished for earthly things: then the mind boils, and inflames itself with the fire of late repentance; then its hardness is melted by torment, hence the prophet: 'Vexation alone shall give understanding to the hearing' (Isaiah 28); they are to suffer this then, meanwhile they are entangled in these things.
6.18: 6.18 They are wrapped up. Everything that is wrapped is folded back on itself: so the wicked, sometimes willing good things, as though stretched outside themselves, are tempted and folded back to their accustomed evils.
