Or they are wrapped, who, although at times, one wickedness being conquered, they lift the foot, another reigning entangles them also in the one they had conquered, so that he who, avarice already scorned, is still luxurious, returns to avarice for the price of luxury. Thus by alternating work the vices hold their fugitive, and bind his going out as with snares, hence they often fall back and return to their pleasures, and do not care for the things that remain, hence he adds: They shall walk in vain and perish. Because they carry nothing with them from the fruit of their labor. But the just man does not appear empty in the sight of the Lord: for he carries the sheaves of justice. From the imitation of those he frightens by the end: Consider the paths, etc.
6.19: 6.19 Consider the paths. Same place. Thema is interpreted 'south wind,' Saba 'net.' The south wind, which loosens the limbs with warmth, is here the lax relaxation of living; the net is the entanglement of action, and a man is entangled by lax actions, while he does not perfectly forsake the world, while he walks not with strict zeal but with loosened steps, as one who, out of carnal love for his parents, is hindered from the things that are God's. Consider, he says, because we love to do perverse things, but when we see them in others we judge them, and so, returning to ourselves, we blush at such things. Wait a little. Because whatever ends is little; but he who thinks this long does not care for eternal things. Having spoken of the brevity of life, he rises against the wicked with the voice of the just.
6.20: 6.20 They are confounded. Because, namely, the wicked try to draw the good back from hope through hardships; if they accomplish it they exult; if not, they blush to have been cruel in vain; hence he adds what happens in the retribution: They also came. At the judgment the wicked come to the just, because they will see their glory, so that they grieve the more heavily seeing what they have lost. Then shame covers them, when conscience as a witness burns. The same spiritually. The friends of Job were confounded, because, while they cannot bend him to despair, they are put to shame; they came when they now recognize the constancy of his mind within and blush. He shows them to be of the number of those who do not fear God except when terrified by their own or others' adversities.
6.21: 6.21 Now you have come, and now seeing my wound. Same place. As if to say: I feared God even before adversities; you, who do not fear God out of love, are afraid only of the lash.
6.22: 6.22 Did I say? The Church does not need the substance of the heretics, whose figure is the friends of Job, that is, carnal wisdom; and she refuses to hear from them the right things which they sometimes say against the devil about conversion, because through these they draw to unfaithfulness. The hand of the enemy is the strength of Satan. The malignant spirits are robust. Did I say: Bring? Against the rich of the world, etc., up to 'and what they despise in themselves, and in others.'
6.24: 6.24 Teach me. This is either joined to what precedes, or is said by itself by way of rebuke.
6.25: 6.25 Why have you detracted? Gregory. He ought to be clean, etc., up to 'do you bring forth things worthy of reproach in order to rebuke?' Same place. Two kinds of speech are harmful: that which both praises perverse things and that which also condemns right ones; there is favor, here anger: of this he accuses the friends of Job; and this vice is reached from idle words, hence he adds:
6.26: 6.26 And into the wind. To utter words into the wind, etc., up to 'let there therefore be a door of the tongue, which is now shut, now opened.'
6.27: 6.27 Upon the fatherless. Gregory, on Job, book 8. Behold, of how great weakness he judges himself to be, etc., up to 'if he tolerates those he does not love, or if he does not tolerate those he loves.'
6.28: 6.28 See whether I lie. Same place. Because, being humble, what he says he does not command by authority but persuades by reason; but because on the occasion of reason opponents are let loose to contention, he adds.
6.29: 6.29 Answer, I beg you, without contention. Because heretics in their inquiries do not aim to attain the truth but to appear victors. And speaking, etc. Because he who speaks is subject to the judgment of the hearer. Let there be an equitable arbiter between his heart and his tongue, so that nothing rushes from the heart through the tongue, but is examined before it is said. And because those who first judge their own words rightly judge the words of others, he adds:
6.30: 6.30 And you will not find in my tongue. Because folly does not sound in me to you, if it does not proceed from your own conscience; so the Church first destroys the falsehoods of enemies, and afterward opens the true things, for which there is no place while falsehoods are held for true; open speech is through the tongue, hidden consideration through the throat, because what the Church preaches outwardly she keeps by living.
7.1: 7.1 And like the days of a hireling. Gregory. He who wishes the days to pass quickly so as to come to the reward of his labor, so is every just man; and as that man sweats in another's labors but prepares his own reward for himself, so let the just man sweat in worldly evils to obtain heavenly goods. He takes care that no day go by empty of work, and the reward be lessened. He suffers hard things so as to be the more crowned, although the wage is already in his heart; yet the heat is felt more heavily in the body, so that afterward there may be refreshment in rest, and this is:
7.2: 7.2 As a servant. Rightly every elect is called a servant, as long as he is under the yoke of this corruption, before he comes into the freedom of glory. And as a hireling. He who would be provoked by the heaviness of the work if he were not relieved by hope of its end, but, that being seen, thinks nothing of what he feels.
7.3: 7.3 Empty months. Of the things of the world, because the good do not seek them by their acts, and they bear laborious nights of adversities, when they are already in the torment of the body. Or empty months, because now there is labor but not yet reward. Laborious nights. He enumerates, etc., up to 'so much the more he groans that he long did not know what he seeks, and that he labored in vain.'
7.4: 7.4 If I lie down to sleep. Same place. According to the history, the mind of one in grief is expressed, who, urged by sadness, wanders through diverse desires; in the night he longs for day, in the day for evening, because sorrow does not let what is present please; and having now found this heavy, consoled by desire he awaits another; but not even so does the sorrow end, hence: And I shall be filled with sorrows. And the cause of the sorrow is this:
7.5: 7.5 My flesh is clothed. Same place. The same more subtly in the Church, etc., up to 'for them salvation is not whole here,' hence he adds: And I shall be filled with sorrows until darkness. Because he does not find security until he wholly leaves the time of temptation. He adds the cause of the sorrow: My flesh is clothed, that is, the carnal life I lead is either polluted by evil working, or, drawn in by it, is darkened by the memory of images of sins, which rise like dust before the eyes. The Church indeed feels the rottenness of the luxury of the flesh in some, among whom, those given to earthly acts, she is sprinkled with dust; of both he adds: My skin. The skin in the Church are those who give themselves only to outward cares: whose hearts despair dries up, and therefore they are drawn together, not stretched by longsuffering toward eternal life: they cling to present things; and this happens because they do not attend how fleeting this life is. But the Church on the contrary:
7.6: 7.6 My days have passed more swiftly. As a web by its threads, so life advances by single days; but the more it grows, the nearer it tends to being cut. The speed of life, which is always failing, even surpasses the haste of the web. And therefore the elect do not fix their heart in it, hence he says: And they are consumed, that is, I put no trust in them: which the reprobate do, I do not.
7.7: 7.7 Remember. Same place. That is, kindly look upon me who am swiftly passing, because the consideration of human brevity is an acceptable offering to God. For my life is wind. Eternal life is solid: this life is judged neither solid nor lasting. Same place. And because after life passes there is no place for earning pardon, he adds: And it shall not return. That is, after death the mind, seeing its retribution, is not recalled to perform good works: hence the rich man, despairing of himself, which is an aggravation of punishment, intercedes for his brothers. Behold, life passes, what follows remains. Afterward also,
7.8: 7.8 Nor shall the eye of man behold me. That is, the mercy of the Redeemer, which softens the hardness of sinners, as when he looked at Peter (Luke 22); but after death he does not free the one whom grace did not reform before. Not the eye of man, but, Your eyes upon. Gregory. That is, you will see the strict judge ready to strike, and he who was waited for here unto repentance will no longer stand. This befits the just man, who fears everything he does, and foreknows that, piety being removed, he will perish, and does not stand before his eyes, because life does not suffice for the penalty if justice presses him. For not even the stars, that is, those who shine with holiness, are clean before him. The guilt and penalty of the human race is briefly added.
18.9: 18.9 His foot shall be held fast, etc. Namely, because his end will be bound up in sin. And thirst shall burn against him. Because the more he judges himself bound to evils, the more he despairs of his return; and by that very despair he seethes the more sharply with the desires of this world. In his mind thirst burns against him, because he who has acted perversely is inflamed to act more perversely.
18.10: 18.10 A snare is hidden in the earth. Same place. A snare is hidden in the earth when guilt is concealed under earthly advantages, so that a man sees what he may be able to desire, and yet by no means sees in what snare of guilt he sets his foot. And his trap. For the enemy observes the character of each, to which vice they are near, and sets before their face those things to which he knows the mind is more easily inclined: luxury for gentle and cheerful characters, anger and pride for harsh minds. He therefore places the trap where he sees the path of the mind to be: because he introduces the danger of deception there where he has found the way of a nearby thought.
18.11: 18.11 Fears shall terrify him on every side. Because often a person fears to be good for this reason, lest he suffer from the wicked what he remembers having done to the good: and while he fears to suffer what he does, terrified on every side, suspected on every side, he loses his step in the good work.
18.12: 18.12 Let his strength be wasted with hunger. Our flesh is weakness. But strength is the rational soul, which is able by reason to resist in fighting the vices. It is wasted with hunger when it is fed by no refreshment of inner food. And let famine invade his ribs. The ribs are the senses of the mind, which protect the hidden thoughts like the inward parts. Famine invades the ribs of the wicked man, because inner hunger weakens the senses of the mind, so that they in no way govern his thoughts within, but wander to the outward things that they seek. Let it devour the beauty of his skin and consume his arms. The same. The beauty of the skin is outward temporal glory; by the arms works are signified. He calls death sin, which kills the soul.
18.13: 18.13 The firstborn death. Pride, which is the beginning of all sin. The firstborn death therefore devours the beauty of his skin and his arms: by which pride supplants the glory or the working of the wicked. For he could have been glorious even in this life, if he had not been proud.
18.14: 18.14 Let his confidence be torn away from his tent. The same. His confidence is torn from his tent when the perverse man, who had prepared many things in this life, is scattered by sudden death. And let destruction tread upon him like a king. Because here he is either oppressed by vices that drag to destruction, or at the time of death is subjected to demonic power.
18.15: 18.15 Let them dwell in his tent. That is, let the apostate angels dwell in his mind through the most wicked thoughts, his companions, that is, who for this reason no longer is, because he has withdrawn from the supreme being. Let it be sprinkled in his tent. Same place. Sulphur is sprinkled in the tent of the wicked as often as the delight of the flesh rules in his mind. For by sulphur the stench of the flesh is understood. And because such a man remains in evil, so that he cannot even produce the fruit of good, he adds:
18.16: 18.16 Let his roots be dried up below. By roots we understand thoughts, etc., down to because all his working is reckoned as nothing by the judgment from above.
18.17: 18.17 Let his memory perish. Same place. The wicked man tries to establish his memory on earth when he strives to extend the glory of his praise. And he rejoices that his name is celebrated in the streets when he spreads the working of his iniquity far and wide. GREGORY. The head of the wicked is the devil: for he in the last times will enter that vessel of perdition which will be called Antichrist, who will try to spread his name far and wide.
18.18: 18.18 He shall drive him out from the light. He is led from light to darkness when he is condemned from the honor of the present life to eternal torments. He speaks thus of each wicked man, so that it turns to the head, that is the devil, who will extend his name in Antichrist, which the wicked now imitate. And he shall remove him from the world, etc. When, with the judge appearing from above, he is transferred from this world to punishments; all of which can also be understood of Antichrist, the head of the wicked.
18.19: 18.19 He shall have no offspring, etc. Because all the wicked, who were born by his persuasion in wicked actions, will be struck down with their same head. Because these things are to be understood of Antichrist, he reveals this when he says:
18.20: 18.20 They shall be astonished at his day. Because he will then display such great signs, etc., down to they fear the torments which they overcome. And horror shall seize the first, that is, the hearts of the elect will be struck with fear; hence it is written: So as to lead into error, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24), not indeed to fall, but to tremble in the flesh.
18.21: 18.21 These then are the tents. He referred to this what he had said, etc., down to because they believed that holy Job was struck for iniquity.
19.2: 19.2 How long do you afflict, etc. GREGORY. The good are worn down by the words of the wicked when those who lie either in perverse faith or in wicked morals swell against them in words.
19.3: 19.3 Behold, ten times you confound me. The same. Because he had heard rebukes from them five times, and had answered five times, he declares that he has been confounded ten times. Because he endured confusion both in being gravely rebuked and in speaking words of doctrine to those who do not listen: in his own rebukes, because he makes no progress in them; in their rebukes, because he grieves at the perversity which he hears. Behold, ten times. The same. The Church keeps the Decalogue, to which the wicked cause confusion as often as they oppose the divine words in their deeds. And you are not ashamed to oppress me. There are some whom malice suddenly arising invites to commit wickedness, but yet human shame calls them back.
19.4: 19.4 Indeed, even if I was ignorant. The knowledge of heretics is not with them but against them, while it puffs up. But the ignorance of the Church, in that it cannot penetrate hidden things, is with it, because it is for it, while it humbles itself; and because what heretics seek to know is elation, so that they may seem learned against the good, he adds: you, on the contrary, should rise up against yourselves, from my being struck, fearing worse things for yourselves. For the good man is first raised against himself, afterward against others.
19.5: 19.5 But you are raised up against me. That is, you leave yourselves to be reproved, and rebuke me with strict sentences. And you reprove me. Because those who had known him to be just before the scourges now judged him unjust from that very striking.
19.6: 19.6 At least now understand. This the Lord had said of him: You have moved me against him in vain, which he himself asserts of himself: that he was not afflicted by the Lord with an equal judgment. For if his life and the scourges are weighed, he seems afflicted with an unequal judgment: but because he heaped up his merits from the scourges, God did not afflict Job with an unjust judgment. Because God not with an equal judgment. It must therefore be maintained that God both dealt rightly with Job, and yet he does not lie who says that it was not done equally: otherwise the devil would have prevailed in what he had promised about the fault of the blessed man whom God praised. This pain, not elation, wrung from him. If a good man in a humble mind, when the cause or grief demands, says good things of himself, he does not sin. And has encompassed me with his scourges. When so great an affliction presses us down that the mind cannot breathe with the consolation of anything, we are no longer merely borne along by scourges, but also encompassed, because we are surrounded on every side by the lash of tribulations.
19.7: 19.7 Behold, I shall cry out suffering violence. The same. God, knowing what will profit us, etc., down to who cannot discern even what is to be done.
19.8: 19.8 He has hedged in my path, etc. He saw his path hedged in with blows when, desiring to pass over to security, he could not escape the scourges: and, as if on the path of the heart, he found darkness of ignorance, since he could not penetrate why he was scourged in this way.
19.9: 19.9 He has stripped me of my glory. These things plainly apply to Job, etc., down to by whose falling the army falls more widely.
19.10: 19.10 He has destroyed me on every side and I perish, and as a tree torn up, etc. A tree is driven by the wind so that it falls: so the weak man is drawn by threats to injustice, and abandons the eternal things he hoped for; and because sometimes he who, terrified by punishments, abandons justice, nevertheless does not escape the punishments.
